case_study_insert.main_stem: Kestrel Ridge Aggregates (KRA) is a private limited company in the quarrying and construction aggregates sector, employing a workforce of 52. Founded in 2007 by Bryn Kestrel, the business supplies crushed stone to regional building contractors and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. KRA plans to invest $720,000 in a recycled-aggregate crushing plant with stormwater recycling, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.00 a unit and a selling price of $14.00, and produces 96,000 units of crushed aggregate a year. KRA faces two operational problems: stone-dust complaints from nearby residents are rising, and labour turnover is increasing among crusher operators.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quarry Operations and Quality Log — Q3 2025: The new screening line processed 24,000 units last quarter at a defect rate of 2.4%, down from 4.1% a year earlier. Customer complaints about stone dust fell from 34 to 19 per month. Average delivery time to building sites is 4.5 days. A survey of 500 local builders found that 61% would pay up to $0.50 more per unit for recycled aggregate, and 47% check a supplier's environmental credentials before ordering. A skills audit shows 14 of 52 operators have not completed on-the-job training on the new crusher; off-the-job courses at the technical college cost $850 per employee.

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.00%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% from $12.60 to $13.33 per hour from April 2026, raising total wage bills. (3) Diesel and tyre input costs for haulage have risen 9.5% year-on-year, while construction output grew 2.8% over the same period.

questions.question_text: KRA plans to fund part of its recycled-aggregate crushing plant with retained profit rather than the $450,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for KRA of using the $270,000 retained profit instead of the loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using $270,000 of retained profit costs KRA no interest charges or capital repayments, which protects cash flow at a time when the business already carries fixed costs of $240,000 a year and a $450,000 ten-year bank loan. Every dollar not paid as interest can instead absorb the 9.5% rise in diesel and tyre costs, helping KRA hold its $14.00 selling price for crushed stone and stay competitive against other quarries supplying regional building contractors. Retained profit also has no fixed repayment timetable, so the $720,000 recycling plant can be commissioned at the quarry's own pace.

Point 2: Retained profit carries no collateral or repossession risk. If demand for recycled aggregate disappoints, the bank cannot seize the new crusher or the quarry site, so Bryn Kestrel's owner-managed company keeps control of its core asset. The bank loan, by contrast, would require security and regular servicing whatever the level of stone-dust complaints or output. Using internal funds also preserves the company's borrowing headroom for later investment in stormwater recycling, and it avoids the lender conditions that could restrict how the 96,000-unit operation is run or expanded.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to KRA's cash flow, costs and ownership.

questions.question_text: KRA is promoting its new recycled aggregate to building contractors. Consider advertising in trade magazines, sponsoring a local building show, or a targeted social media campaign. Which should KRA choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Trade magazine advertising: A trade magazine reaches building contractors directly and gives KRA space to explain the recycled content and stormwater recycling of the new plant, which matters to the 47% of surveyed builders who check environmental credentials. It is a credible, permanent medium for technical claims. However, a full-page campaign is expensive for a 52-employee quarry already servicing a $450,000 loan, the audience is narrower than the regional contractor base KRA supplies, and print cannot demonstrate the product or respond to the 61% of builders who would pay $0.50 more until long after the $720,000 plant is running.

Local building show sponsorship: A stand at a local show lets KRA meet contractors face to face, hand over samples of recycled aggregate and answer questions about quality, directly tackling the stone-dust complaints by showing the stormwater system. It is cheaper than national print and builds relationships in KRA's own region. Its weakness is reach: a three-day event touches only the contractors who attend, so it cannot by itself sell enough of the 96,000 units the quarry produces, and the cost per order can be high.

Targeted social media campaign: Paid social ads can be aimed at regional contractors and sustainability-focused builders, showing short videos of the crushing line and linking the 61% premium finding to a clear $0.50 message. It is measurable, scalable and cheap per contact, and can be adjusted quickly if the 2.4% defect rate or delivery times of 4.5 days need explaining. It depends on builders actually using the platforms and on sustained spend to keep visibility.

Recommendation: KRA should choose the targeted social media campaign. It reaches the exact segment identified in the 500-builder survey, costs far less than trade print, and scales regionally in a way a single local show cannot. The building show is rejected as too limited in reach; trade magazines are rejected as costly and slow. KRA should use the show only as a low-cost supporting opportunity.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to KRA.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of KRA with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of KRA with a well-justified recommendation explaining why trade magazines and the building show are rejected.

questions.question_text: KRA's autocratic leadership sits in a hierarchical structure, and labour turnover among its 52 operators is rising. Explain two benefits for KRA of introducing a more democratic leadership style.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives KRA's 52 operators a voice in how the recycled-aggregate crusher is run, so the people closest to the stone-dust problem can suggest practical changes to screening routines and shift patterns. Under the present autocratic, hierarchical approach, operators simply follow instructions and disengage; involving them raises job satisfaction and commitment, which directly addresses the rising labour turnover and protects the 96,000-unit output needed to justify the $720,000 plant.

Point 2: Consulting operators draws on their experience of the new crusher and the 14 staff still without on-the-job training, generating ideas that reduce the current 2.4% defect rate and the complaints that fell from 34 to 19 per month. Workers who help set quality routines are more likely to follow them, lowering rework and waste. Higher involvement also makes KRA more attractive to skilled workers in a tight regional labour market, cutting the cost and disruption of repeatedly recruiting and training replacements for a workforce already stretched by the new line.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to KRA's turnover, defects and output.

questions.question_text: KRA must upskill 14 of its 52 operators on the new crusher. Consider on-the-job training at the quarry or off-the-job courses at the technical college at $850 per employee. Which should KRA choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching at the crusher is directly relevant to KRA's own screening line and quality standards, costs no college fees, and keeps the 14 operators productive while they learn, which protects the 24,000 units processed last quarter and the improvement from a 4.1% to a 2.4% defect rate. Experienced operators can demonstrate the exact routines that reduce stone-dust complaints. The drawback is that the trainers are themselves production staff, so their output falls while coaching; bad habits can be passed on; and there is no external certificate, which may matter when the 47% of builders who check environmental credentials ask for evidence of competence.

Off-the-job training: The technical college course at $850 per employee would cost $11,900 for all 14 staff (14 × $850), a modest sum against the $720,000 investment. It gives structured, up-to-date instruction and a recognised qualification that supports KRA's environmental claims to builders. However, it removes 14 of 52 operators from the quarry, cutting capacity during commissioning, and the generic content will not match KRA's exact crusher settings, so follow-up coaching on site would still be required.

Decision: KRA should choose on-the-job training first, with short college top-ups later. It is cheaper, machine-specific and avoids losing output while labour turnover is already rising; full off-the-job training is rejected because taking 14 operators away and spending $11,900 would disrupt the 96,000-unit schedule for skills that still need on-site adaptation.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to KRA.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of KRA.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of KRA with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how KRA's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $240,000 ÷ ($14.00 − $8.00) = $240,000 ÷ $6.00 = 40,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 40,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $14.00 − $8.00 = $6.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $6.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways KRA's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing the 40,000-unit break-even point with actual output of 96,000 units shows a margin of safety of 56,000 units (96,000 − 40,000), confirming the quarry can absorb a demand fall and helping managers judge whether to run the new crusher at full capacity.
2. Contribution of $6.00 a unit lets managers model price moves: a $0.50 discount to $13.50 leaves $5.50 contribution, and 40,000 units would then only just cover $240,000 of fixed costs, so discount decisions can be tested before they are offered to builders.
3. The same figures set the sales target needed to service the $450,000 bank loan and justify the $720,000 plant: 40,000 units cover fixed costs, and every unit above that adds $6.00 toward returns.
4. Unit cost data ($240,000 ÷ 96,000 units + $8.00 = $10.50 a unit) allows quarter-by-quarter benchmarking of the screening line, highlighting the waste and defect problems so management can act on the 2.4% defect rate and 9.5% input-cost rise.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 40,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $6.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 56,000 units against 96,000-unit output; discount modelling against $240,000 fixed costs; loan-service feasibility for the $720,000 plant; and unit-cost benchmarking at $10.50 to tackle defects and input inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate KRA's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.5%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 15.0%
ROCE 2025 = 18.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit of $528,000 on revenue of $1,320,000 gives 528 ÷ 1,320 = 0.400; 2025 gross profit of $648,000 on $1,440,000 gives 648 ÷ 1,440 = 0.450. Operating profit of $165,000 ÷ $1,320,000 = 0.125 and $216,000 ÷ $1,440,000 = 0.150. Returns on the $1,100,000 and $1,200,000 capital employed are 165 ÷ 1,100 = 0.150 and 216 ÷ 1,200 = 0.180.

Evaluation: Every measure moved favourably. The 40.0% to 45.0% rise in the first margin shows KRA kept cost of sales at $792,000 while revenue grew by $120,000, so additional crushed-stone sales were earned without extra input cost. The 12.5% to 15.0% rise in operating profitability shows fixed costs of $240,000 were absorbed more effectively as output rose, and the 15.0% to 18.0% return on capital shows the asset base is being used more productively. Against this, interest payable rose from $18,000 to $22,000, and a $450,000 loan plus a $720,000 plant means future returns could be competed away if the 9.5% diesel and tyre inflation continues. The 47% of builders checking credentials also means some of the revenue gain may depend on maintaining the eco positioning.

Conclusion: KRA's performance has improved. Higher revenue, unchanged cost of sales and rising operating profit lift both margins and the return on capital, so the business is more profitable and uses its assets better. The main risk is rising interest and input costs, which management should watch, but on the 2024–2025 evidence the improvement is genuine and broad-based.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three profitability measures for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost of sales, capital employed and interest movements and a justified conclusion on whether performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for KRA of producing recycled aggregate at its new crushing plant.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Recycled aggregate matches the survey evidence that 61% of the 500 builders questioned would pay up to $0.50 more per unit, allowing KRA to protect the $6.00 contribution per unit on its $8.00 variable cost even as diesel and tyre costs rise 9.5%. It also appeals to the 47% who check environmental credentials, supporting the $720,000 investment by strengthening relationships with the regional contractors who buy the 96,000 units the quarry produces.

Disadvantage: Producing recycled aggregate can require extra sorting and screening, which would push up the $8.00 variable cost per unit and squeeze margins unless the full $0.50 premium is accepted. Contamination in reclaimed material may also raise the current 2.4% defect rate and worsen stone-dust complaints, risking the delivery record of 4.5 days while the new line is still bedding in and labour turnover among operators is rising.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to KRA's survey data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.00%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 9.5% rise in diesel and tyre costs will affect KRA. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.00%): If the $450,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $450,000 = $3,375 a year (0.0075 × $450,000). That is small beside fixed costs of $240,000 and can be removed by fixing the rate; if the loan is already fixed, the direct effect is zero. Higher rates could still make future borrowing for the $720,000 plant dearer.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $13.33 an hour): KRA employs a workforce of 52, many of them crusher operators, so wage costs will rise and cannot be avoided. The insert gives neither hours worked nor individual pay, so no defensible annual wage total can be calculated. The honest comparison is with productivity: 96,000 units ÷ 52 workers ≈ 1,846 units per worker a year, so the rise is affordable only if output per worker holds or improves; otherwise unit labour cost climbs and the $6.00 contribution shrinks.

Diesel and tyre costs (9.5%): Haulage is central to delivering crushed stone to builders. The $8.00 variable cost is not broken down in the insert, so only a labelled upper bound can be shown: if the whole variable cost rose 9.5%, that adds 0.095 × $8.00 = $0.76 per unit; across 96,000 units that is $72,960 a year (96,000 × $0.76). Even a smaller pass-through would cut contribution from $6.00 toward roughly $5.24 and threaten the returns needed to justify the new plant.

Conclusion: The 9.5% rise in diesel and tyre costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 96,000 units sold, directly erodes the contribution that funds the $450,000 loan and the $720,000 investment, and cannot be neutralised by a one-off action. The interest rise is quantifiably small at $3,375 and can be fixed, while the wage effect depends on hours that are not given and can be offset by productivity, so both are smaller threats.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to KRA.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on KRA's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of KRA with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
